utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody and to you, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps just one small administrative matter before we call the witness in. Yesterday Mr. Petrovic agreed to introduce as an exhibit the video of Mr. Grbic who has already testified before the Tribunal. Perhaps if I can take this opportunity to provide -- to tender the exhibit itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask if this will be received as a Prosecution Exhibit or Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Prosecution by consent of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I don't think there's an objection to the -- its --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let it be the exhibit of the OTP; I don't mind. What we are interested in are the photographs from this particular exhibit, which are things that the Chamber has heard a number of times already. Whatever Mr. Kaufman considers to be expeditious. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Let it not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Kaiser. If I could remind you once again of the affirmation you took which still applies. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kaiser. Please tell me: This commission of experts which was set up by the security council, whom did it assist of? Who were the members of this commission? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. You're asking me about the commission of experts. I had dealings with the -- with a team of experts. I don't know if it's exactly the same thing as the commission of experts. The commission of experts was a little wider body.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So I'm asking you about those people with whom you prepared a part of the report of the commission of experts which has to do with events in and around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The members of the team, there was a Canadian named -- an officer named Dominic McAlea. And then there were two Norwegian lawyers and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall the names of these Norwegians?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm sorry. I can't recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was perhaps one of the interior Lund and the other one Oyvind Hoel? If I pronounce the names correctly?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you know these people I assume in person, since you did this work together?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have some memories of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you travel anywhere together?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we travelled together. We travelled from Zagreb to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend together in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So I presume that you got could well acquainted, that you had occasion to discuss various things associated with your work, not only your work because of which you came to Dubrovnik in the first place?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we were together quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: Were these Norwegian lawyers members -- or do you hold any opinions of these lawyers? Are these serious people, responsible people, who did their duties in a very conscientious way, in your view?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were very, very serious people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if I understood this correctly, this was a project where the project leader was Sharif Basuni [phoen] and you were just part of one of the working bodies that was part of this overall project. Was that not so?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In view of what you said a while ago about your colleagues, the Norwegian lawyers, would you agree with me that if these were, as you said, serious people, that what they said to the investigators of this Tribunal certainly merits to be lent credence in terms of the correctness, the truthfulness, of what they stated to them?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have before me a statement which Mr. Hoel Oyvind gave to the investigators of the international Tribunal, discussing precisely these topics that we talked about yesterday here. And I would like to ask you in that connection whether a statement which he -- whether an assertion which he makes or several of his assertions he makes in that connection. In his statement to an investigator of the Tribunal, Dirk Hooijkaas, which he gave in March 2001 and April 2002. Speaking about the mandate of your commission, Mr. Oyvind said the following: "Our task was to establish whether their existed the sufficient evidence for putting on trial war criminals and to identify those who had perpetrated war crimes." Did Mr. Oyvind correctly describe the purpose and the mandate of your mission as part of the commission of experts?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall today, in view of this given definition of that mission, can you remember today in respect of the other part of the mission's task what the -- what was the conclusion, namely the task, the second task, the question of those who were responsible?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what their conclusion was. You must remember that I was taken there specifically about the damaging to the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I was under the impression, Your Honours, that there had been a ruling on this matter yesterday, namely that this commission of experts report would not be brought through the back door to the Chamber's attention without a proper submission as to how it could be submitted. Now, I understood Mr. Petrovic yesterday as not requesting that that commission of experts' report be tendered as an exhibit, therefore I would object to the conclusions of that particular report being brought to the Chamber's attention by questions asked to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me. I'm not raising this question in order to prejudge anything which would be the attitude of this Chamber. I'm just asking the witness whether he remembers what the result of his work was. If he doesn't remember it, I will move on. I don't see anything questionable in that, but as my learned colleague says, I myself see no reason for exhibiting that particular report at this point. But if you feel that I am devoting too much time to it, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you should move on, Mr. Petrovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Kaiser, have you ever heard of the name Zeljko Soldo?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me who is this man and how did you hear about him.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about him in fact when I was in Dubrovnik with the team of the commission of experts, because Zeljko Soldo had been a -- I think a Herzegovinian Croat officer who had been in the federal forces and had in fact been, not captured, but he had been taken prisoner later on after the shelling of Dubrovnik and he had been brought to trial by a Croatian tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me what kind of contacts did your mission have with this man.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no contact with him, but I believe that -- I think two -- because I think he was in prison, in fact, in Dubrovnik, that two of the members of the team in fact went to visit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And is it true, is it true what Mr. Oyvind said when he says that the commission relied very extensively on the stance of the Croatian army in connection with the war doctrine of the Yugoslav People's Army, that it didn't have any authentic, original sources of knowledge but that in connection with that particular issue, it replied on what was given it by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't wish to sound like a broken record, but I think I have already made my objection to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, what the commission might have found or not found in that early preliminary report does not appear likely to be of any assistance to this Chamber when it comes to consider what the evidence led here reveals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I think the time you're spending on that is not valuable for any purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to spend another minute on it. My apologies, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, you told us that you had never seen anyone who was a member of the Croatian army. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the period when you made these visits to Dubrovnik, 1991, 1992, and 1993 -- rather, in 1991 and 1993 as things seem to stand now.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 1991 when I was in a mission for UNESCO and in 1993 when I was on mission for the commission of experts. In 1991 I mentioned that we did see some soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you had a personal contact with any of the members of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a personal contact with members of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Miso Mihocevic?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by that name and surname? This is a captain of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may have been somebody we met in 1993. There may have been -- listen, I'm not very good on this name, all right? But there was some sort of liaison officer I think we met in 1993, not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think Mr. Petrovic knows just as well as I do -- Your Honours don't know this because Mr. Petrovic has the statement in front of him, that this does in fact refer to 1993 and an incident within the context of the commission of experts' report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I think my colleague is exaggerating a bit. I'm not asking anything about the report of the commission of experts; I'm asking him about his acquaintance with people who were officers of the Croatian army. That has nothing to do with the commission's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Petrovic, on that limited basis. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you saw this person, this man, for the first time in 1993. Right?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing this man in 1993. I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why then does Mr. Oyvind say the following in his statement: "Your commission met when it came with Captain Miso Mihocevic. He was, he says a liaison officer, to liaise between the United Nations and the Croatian army. And then he goes on to say that "I found out that the captain had had personal contacts with Mr. Kaiser on his previous trips."

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This captain had had contacts -- this Croatian army officer had had contacts with Mr. Kaiser on his previous trips. I did not have any contact with a Croatian army officer on previous trips.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me then: Why would Mr. Oyvind state such an untruthful fact in his statement? What reason would he have to do so?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we met lots of people, lots of civilians, in 1991. If some of these civilians - and I can't remember this gentleman - if some of these civilians turned out to be army officers later, that's one thing. But I do not remember meeting a Croatian officer, this gentleman, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So for you, a member of the army is only a person who wears a uniform. You cannot have a person who perhaps is not wearing a uniform, whether that someone meets with you. Can that someone be a member of the army anyway?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that person tells me he's a member of the army and he's not wearing his uniform, then I assume he's a member of the army. If he's wearing a uniform, then I also assume he's a member of the army without him having to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If the person doesn't say anything to you and does not wear a uniform, you conclude that the person is not a member?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Or you perhaps conclude or you conclude that perhaps that person became a member later?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if a person doesn't say anything to me and he's not wearing a uniform and a third person doesn't tell me that this person is a member of the army, then for me he's not a member of the army. If a person whom I may have met - and I can't remember meeting this man in 1991 - if later this person becomes a member of the army, and I meet him, and he's a member of the army in 1993, and he's in a uniform, yes, he's a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: If you didn't see this person in 1991, when did you see him? In 1993 you said that you -- you say that you had seen that person before, and when was it in the meanwhile that you learned about this person, Miso Mihocevic?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all we're trying to see if I met this person, and I vaguely remember the name. And then I do remember meeting an army officer, a liaison officer in 1993. And that's it. I didn't meet him before, as far as I can remember. I can't remember this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you submit that Mr. Oyvind is stating an untruthful fact for a reason known to him?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not stating he's making an untruthful statement. I'm stating that I have not -- I have no memory of meeting this person before, that is in 1991; I remember meeting him in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who was the liaison officer in 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have a liaison officer. We did not have any dealing with Croatian officers and we had no liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who did the duties of the interpreter at that time, do you perhaps remember, between the authorities, which is to say the Crisis Staff and the international authorities and the other officials in the city of Dubrovnik in 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had an interpreter named Vesna Gamulin who accompanied us everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to examine police files related to 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about 1993 and the commission of experts again, sir. There were -- there was a certain amount of information that was made available by local authorities to the commission -- to the team that was working for the commission of experts in 1993. And I recall getting a very brief glimpse of photographs of bodies, a very brief glimpse because I don't like those things, and I think that those were police photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why does Mr. Oyvind say then that you and Mr. Lund inspected police files for a full three days in Dubrovnik, and those police files related to 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I indicated that I think that I did see police files. I can't remember if I had looked at police files for three days in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Why would someone show to you, a Ph.D. Holder, historian files with dead bodies? What connection does that have to do with your line of duty?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just happened to be with the lawyer that particular day. I don't know what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you what connection is there between your own job and the examination of photographs of dead bodies for a full three days?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered you, sir. I was a member of the commission. I could be asked to go somewhere and look for Red Cross files or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you practically worked on all sorts of jobs, both those falling within your particular line of activity and those which were outside of your own field of competence?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did different things, but I was particularly dealing with the questions of the damaging to the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you for the last time: Why would someone show to you photographs of dead people in the police station when you were in charge of assessing damage done to the Old City?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you have to realise something. When you're done for a couple of weeks and there's four of you and you're trying to get your hands on as much information as possible, you can't say, I'm sorry, I only deal with the destruction of cultural heritage. I don't want to see anything else. You're a member of a team and you have to help the team do its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Even if you didn't know anything about that particular area of work, still you would give them a hand, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would help them out if it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to make a remark. Yesterday I spoke about P62, it's a Prosecution exhibit -- or rather P63. I referred to it as P62 and I was corrected. It was P63 and whenever I made a reference to P62 yesterday, what I had in mind actually was P63. I wish to make that clear, first of all, Your Honours, and my apologies to everyone in the courtroom. And now if the witness can please be shown P51 and P63.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, can you please have a look at P63, tab 6. This is your report. I am not sure about the dates. Can you please look at the introduction, or rather, the letter that you wrote on the 14th of October 1993. That's page 1 of the letter, page 36. That's how the letter begins, towards the bottom half of the first page of the letter. You speak about your reasons and concerns as a human being, about your helplessness to protect the people of Dubrovnik. Please explain: Did you have any compunction about these things? Why did you voice these sentiments in relation to what you talked about? You were an expert after all, you were there as an expert free from bias, you were there to ascertain what was going on. Why these emotional and sentimental outpourings that we can find on page 1 of your letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see my -- read my emotional and sentimental outpourings, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Paragraph 8 of page 1, the letter is dated 14th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in connection with the so-called planned three-day bombardment, sir. I mention the terrible shock I experienced at 5.48 a.m. on 6th of December of having abysmally failed to protect the people of Dubrovnik. Sir, may I indulge in a little bit of sentimental and emotional comment now to explain the remark? On the morning of that bombardment, I was extremely shocked when I realised that it seemed that the shells were coming on the town, I did have a sense, a very strong sense, that the mission had failed. And the three flags we had run up over the town and the fact that there was shooting going on was a failure. Sir, I did not believe that there would be a bombardment. I was so confident that the three flags and that the word that was given, these things would succeed in saving the town, and I felt that we failed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it's your conscience that causes this concern?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps feel a need to repay someone for something that you were supposed to do and failed to do back then, at the time?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in the days I was going around in the town looking in the -- looking in the houses and being with the people, I also felt something else, and that was shame. And I think when we're talking about failure and we're talking about shame, we're talking about a sort of universal human emotion. And I think that nearly everybody -- I know my colleague, Mr. Carnez, felt something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you on that count, sir. Can you please look at B.1, item 1. It's the section which is about The Hague Convention signs. Can you just tell me briefly: Why was it that you didn't mention in this section what you had seen before you arrived in Dubrovnik, The Hague flag being flown on top of Srdj. You had seen that, but you make no reference to it here. Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mention I had seen it on a video. This was about the sign of The Hague Convention in town. I was writing about the town. You remember that the mission was in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, of course, that your mission was in town. But this feature where there was a lot of fighting going on all the time is just outside town in the immediate vicinity, so I've been wondering why was this something that you did not think was worth including in your report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you also remember that I said I had seen it on a video taken I don't know how many days before, and that when I was in Dubrovnik I didn't -- I also didn't see it. I can also remind you of that. But the main point is: I was to talk about what was going on in the town and how the town was defended. This is part of a description of protection measures taken in the Old Town of Dubrovnik. This is about the flag. Other parts are about what the locals had done to protect their heritage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Tell me, sir: In connection with item B, 1 and 2, this is your proposal to give the enemy a list of buildings marked and protected under The Hague Convention. Is that what it says, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: B.1.2 correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: B, item 1 and item 2. The heading is: "Proposal Related to the 1954 Convention."

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I indicate it was important -- that there should be communication of information, and I say to the enemy and to UNESCO a list of monuments that are marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in this particular situation, such a list was never actually forwarded to the other side?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mention afterwards, [French phrase spoken], this seems not to have been done for Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at C.1.1. now. All I want is for you to confirm the truthfulness of this, that the chronology of shelling was vague in the memories of the inhabitants of Dubrovnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, at this time one of the things that we discovered very, very often when we went around is the fact that people knew exactly the day that their house was hit; this was something that they really, they really seemed to remember. Later on, these dates, they do tend to slip out of mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say: "It's interesting to observe that the citizens of Dubrovnik often speak of four or five days of shelling of the Old Town in November, which also may be the psychological impact of the shelling itself on the citizens."

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What they're vague about -- they're vague about the chronology; they're not vague about when their own house was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at the section C.1.2. You say that projectiles most frequently -- the projectile most frequently used during the shelling was the 82-millimetre shell fired from Stalin's organ." So this seems to be corrected later on, Stalin's organ, and what was inserted in its place was Stalin VBR. Can you tell me, first of all, which of the two is correct and then what is a VBR.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see that written on this particular document. I see indeed that a Stalin organ has been struck out. And then I see [French phrase spoken], and something else a little bit written in the margin which I can't read.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. My apologies, sir. Which document are you looking at, the French one or the English one?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at my report, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Please tell me what it said there and what the correction was that you inserted and how the correction came about, sir.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't remember at what moment this particular correction was put it, but it removes the Stalin organs and -- frankly what's written here in English is not very good. "The projectile most frequently found for these bombardments, 24 targets acta [phoen] hit which were seen by the observers was a shell of 82-millimetres shot in Rafel [phoen] from shell of 82 millimetres." It doesn't make a great deal of sense with the correction put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it's a mistranslation probably, isn't it, into English, I mean?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This looks like a mistake, not a correction. We have a mistake first of all in the original text and now we have another mistake in the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what is actually correct in the whole thing? What's truthful? If we look beyond translation problems in English and in B/C/S. Which of the dates given here are actually truthful? What's your position on that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about this 82-millimetre projectile. A little bit later on in the paragraph it says in English: "For the population it was called a rocket." In other words we're talking about the rocket which was a 82-millimetre shell, that was a cylinder, which had little wings that folded out when it was shot, and that's what we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Sir, can you please look at C.2.1, the heading is: "The report of the Institute for the Protection of Cultural and Historical Monuments."

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please look at paragraph 2 which says: "Accurate assessments have been made, but very often all they offer is mere impressions of what had occurred." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Evaluation containing the report of this institute are of good quality but often impressionistic." Shall we continue? Say where.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. All I want to know is this first sentence; what does that actually mean?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would -- they didn't do things like indicate -- try to find out what the shells were. They weren't very exact about what types of fragments were shot about. They were a little general in their mention of the damage often -- not all the time, but often.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you still agree with the fact that their reports often seem to contain political propaganda? Would I be right in concluding that, based on your other sentences in the same paragraph?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's put it this way: There was something that they didn't bring up, which in fact could really indeed could be considered to be political propaganda. On Fort Minceta, there were a number of impacts of the 82-millimetre rocket, and these were close to the windows. Now these -- on Fort St. John there were a number of refugees who were living in the fort. It was said everywhere in the town that, in fact, the federal artillerymen had deliberately been shooting at the windows to try to put a shell through the window and to try to hurt the refugees. Now, they didn't mention this in their report, and I thought this was a pretty good example of trying to be even-handed and objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does your remark mean that there was a lot of political propaganda involved in the whole thing? You refer to their report, not to it actually going on in town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It's necessary to recall outside of any question -- political question of propaganda, that it was very difficult on the psychological level for the architects", et cetera, et cetera. This is -- just keep it aside, because it was not -- it wasn't a problem in this particular -- in this report. Political propaganda was not a problem in their preliminary report. What was a problem was that it was not precise enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please have a look at Exhibit P51; that's the preliminary report. Book 1, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you look at insula Z as it relates to the town walls, that's Z24, right at the beginning. Did you compile these minutes on damage assessment?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked -- I compiled some minutes of damage assessments; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about this specific one?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember which ones I did exactly. I did a bunch, and then I went and did a lot of other things. I don't -- I don't know -- I don't remember where the tower of St. Franjo in fact is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, these minutes clearly reflect that you compiled them yourself, don't they?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I compiled them back in December 1991. I don't have minutes of these. I don't have any of these materials anymore. I worked on these and handed them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this document which seems to bear your signature, your signature as the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a typed-up version of notes that would have been handed in to the members of the institute of a survey that I carried out with Mr. Franic on this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this is your report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they have put -- they have not put my name on it in such -- when in fact it shouldn't be on. This is our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at Z25. Did you do that, too?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the English edition --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the English edition says it's Mr. Franic that did it. And I don't remember doing it, and I think it's just Mr. Franic that did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The B/C/S version - unfortunately I don't have the English text right now - seems to indicate that you did not sign this document, but your name is there. So probably this is not correct, and maybe the translation is not appropriate. But what the B/C/S version seems to reflect is your name there, Colin Kaiser, historian.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems that my name has been left out from the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I indicate the copy which the Chamber has does include your name, Dr. Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry Z27?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, this one has -- yes, this one has my name on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That doesn't tell us anything, the fact that your name is there. It doesn't jog your memory in any way, does it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to think of where the church of St. Spas is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there's nothing you know about that, we may as well move on, sir. All right. Let's move on, then. Can you please look at book 2 now, same document. Can you please look at insula 8-36. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at it. I'm trying to remember Gariste 2. I'm sorry, sir, I don't remember the names of these little streets. This was a very, very long time ago. Something else that -- well, there are no pictures. Pictures often help one to remember things, and there are no documents around here that have any pictures in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at all which section of the town we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is 8 and this would be -- this section would be in fact south of the Stradun.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why is your signature not there if you were the one who compiled this?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir -- okay, I'm looking at the English edition, the English translation, it's typed. It doesn't indicate the individual documents I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness the B/C/S version of the same document, P51, book 2. The pages 01069521.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's got -- it's okay. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Franic signed this?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is your signature?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My signature is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why isn't your signature there if you really were the one who put this document together?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were very busy, and we simply forgot to sign it. This is -- remember, this is another thing, this is another kind of document -- this is a transcription on to clean form of a form of -- that was filled out, and I don't know if anybody has original forms. I would suspect there would be signatures on the original ones as well. This one, maybe I simply never got around to signing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this is the original of the damage report, or is this a document that's no original at all? If this is no original, then what sort of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are the transcriptions from the surveys that were carried out, and this is the original report that would be submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which language did you use in the drafting of the original report, which doesn't appear to be this report we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what language did we use on the original forms? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this is not the original report. We do agree on that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the original form, but this is said to be the preliminary report and it's presented as the preliminary report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, sir, tell me: The original form, which language did you write it in?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but it's -- I -- I simply can't remember. I was with Mr. Franic. Maybe I wrote some of them in English; maybe he wrote some of them in Serbo-Croatian. I simply cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign that, what was written in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we signed the original forms, the rough forms that we filled out. But there don't seem to be any available for verification. And this is why those would come down -- this why they would -- the signatures and the names would appear on this clean version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this is the revised, purified version of what you originally put down and compiled.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say clean not purified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you leave this one, Mr. Petrovic, am I correct in seeing the signature of Mr. Franic with a date of 2000 against it, rather than 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also believe that you're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just an additional reason why it is not clear why the original documents which were compiled are not there, but rather documents that were signed and given in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if I may be of assistance in this matter, whether this is in fact the appropriate time to raise the issue, but since Your Honour did in fact raise the matter, I would respectfully request Your Honours to remember the evidence of Ms. Peko in this respect, that she was presented with the reports when she was interviewed by investigators of the OTP and she signed the reports that she had herself dealt with. So, of course, it may not be the appropriate place to submit this, but I would also submit that this is what happened. I believe Mr. Franic was also interviewed by the investigators of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would simply observe, Mr. Petrovic, that there are many signatures throughout the B/C/S version. They all appear to have a date in 2000 or perhaps one or two in 2001. Now, all I can see at the moment appear to have a 2000 date. So there appears no signature in 1991 on any form that I've quickly seen in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. We cannot hear counsel. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Your Honour, you are right. There does not exist a single signature on these documents from 1991, except for this signature on the introductory text of the first section of the Croatian version of this document. There are no other original signatures there. There is a signature of the director of the institute Dorotea Valjalo and that is all as far as signatures on these documents are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honour? May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can, but that signature also appears to be dated July 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I thought that at least that one was an original signature, in view of the date, the 6th of January, and given the fact that this is written in this little square here. But it is quite correct. My apologies again. This is only further argumentation to substantiate my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think it's a matter of apology, Mr. Petrovic. It seems quite clear that generally speaking none of these documents were signed in 1991 by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Kaiser, can we at all talk again -- I want to talk with you about these reports at all. Do you anything -- who can assist me with establishing the actual truth if you don't know anything about them. Whom am I to ask about them? Can you help me there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to help you. As you well know, I mean, we were involved in setting up the methodology of the reports -- a survey, and the survey was to be carried out -- well, we carried out a little bit of it ourselves, but then an overwhelming majority of it was carried out by the members of the institute and the volunteers that they brought in. I assume you can certainly ask the people who actually carried out them -- the mass of the work, you can ask them about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. But if it says on this report that you did it, that -- when your name features in some 30-odd of these reports, of the 500 which there existed in all -- although I would have every reason to ask you about the other 470, once I will not do so, I will not take time out of this time that we have allotted. But I'm asking you about this small number which does bear your name. And please tell me: Is it true or not that you are unable to tell me anything about it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I had to chance to look at all my entries which I worked on, if I had a chance to have a map of Dubrovnik, and if I had access to the photographs, then I could tell you something about them, sir. I didn't take -- I have no notes from this, my own notes. I made this point already. I have extensive, copious notes for the survey made on -- for October and November which I kept, because that was a minor issue after the 6th of December. I have no original documents, except there are a lot of photographs taken by me which were -- which are not in the annex but which were presented to UNESCO with very -- with captions. There are hundreds of photographs. I don't have those photographs in my possession; they are in the possession of UNESCO. I could help you, sir, if I had access to all this information. Flipping through things all the time is not very helpful for refreshing the memory, I'm sorry to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you cannot tell me anything about this. When I say this is not true, you say you don't know anything about it. So should we move on.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't want to look at every single form, which may or may not refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right then, will you please take a look at 8-31. That's a bit forward. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just, please, go to the English version of it. I'm sorry, sir, I don't remember where this is exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you take a look in this same book, 11-29. Do you know anything about this one?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where this street is. I think I know where it is, because it's near the church, Domino. You're asking me if I remember ricochetting shrapnel that caused minor damage to the cover. Blast -- for stability. I don't remember any fragment damage. It's hard to remember these things, I think you would appreciate. This is the locality I think I remember a little bit better, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at what you have done, Mr. Kaiser. In those reports where there is --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry that's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where -- in respect of those reports which do bear your signature, you don't remember anything. And as regards this one where there is no signature of yours, you're telling me what kind of damage was sustained. So you're improvising, sir.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I wasn't improvising. I was reading what was written here. And I was saying that I remember base -- roughly where this is. But I don't remember this damage; this was written -- this is done by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at 12-1, sir. Let me warn you right away. There -- it has your signature, so you need not be concerned about whether this is something that doesn't have your signature so that you need to resort to eloquency in order to reply to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I quite understood Mr. Petrovic's last remark. It certainly didn't seem to be in the form of a question. "You need to resort to eloquency in order to reply to my question," it seems more of a remark of a sarcastic nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: An inappropriate one, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the witness and to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember where the Poljana Paska Street is. This is an important building, a large structure, and I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Here you establish that a guided missile was the shell that actually inflicted the damage. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's mentioned that this was the -- that this was actually -- well, that's what it was attributed to, one of the shells. I don't remember...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please then find -- you said that -- where it says the type of shell it says "guided rocket, guided missile," so please read this text and tell me where in this text there is a single reference to any guided missile having hit this building here.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I will read it. You are correct, it does not say. It does not say specifically that this particular missile did any of the particular type of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: With relation to this building it says MB 120 millimetres up here. How many hits were there? Do you know that? Why isn't the number of hits indicated?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't remember doing this particular work. The -- I would just -- excuse me, I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you weren't there at all on that particular site?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in Dubrovnik; I wasn't in Paris. I would just point out that the text does indicate the different mortar impacts, in the first sentence, for example. But it does say things like "several" on the second page. I'm looking also at this English version --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps find any fragments of any shell of any rocket?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, I don't remember doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, sir, take a look at - if you will - 12-3. Let us dispense with the description of the damage, which you probably do not recall. Let us just look -- will you please look at the date and hour when this damage was established. It says -- or actually, this report was compiled. It says that it was done on the 9th of December at 12.17.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreter apologies terribly. Can you hear me now? Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the date and the hour. Is it true that it says the 9th of December, 12.17?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now look at the following, 12-4, does it say the 9th of December, 12.20?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The next one, 12-5, does it say 9th of December, 12.30?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't have 12-5.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It is right behind it, the very next page.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found the Serbo-Croatian version. And you're right, it does give a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it's 12.30. Right? Now look at 12-6, 9th of December, 12.40. And then take a look at the next one, 12-7. The 9th of December, 12.46. The previous one finished in 6 minutes. Then look at the next one, 12-8, the 9th of December, 12.50. In 33 minutes six buildings, of which some for four minutes and some or six minutes, came under this -- were inspected. Can, Mr. Kaiser, this inspection be carried out in four minutes or six minutes, an on-the-scene inspection of any structure. Is that at all possible of any, any, any matter? Would this be a truly serious effort and report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that these kinds of timings are really -- sort of more indicative then in fact really, really realistic or even exact. You know, some things can be done very quickly, if it involves simply shell fragments on a facade, that kind of thing. I mean, some things take indeed much, much longer. If this is a question of little damage, they can be done fairly quickly, but I wouldn't guarantee that those are the exact times that things were actually seen and inspected. I notice that everywhere there's an attempt -- well, not everywhere, but there's an attempt to do this, not just Mr. Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look. Let's go back to 12-3. This is the third category of damage. So you entered the building. You looked at the building from outside, 12-3 is the one I'm talking about. You looked at the building from outside. The building has three storeys. Obviously there is damage to the roof. And the next inspection was carried out by Mr. Franic and yourself on Iza Roka Street at 12.20, which means that you had completed the previous task in all of three minutes. You looked at the building from outside, you entered the building, you examined the building from the inside, you climbed up to the third floor in order to ascertain if there was any damage on the third floor, and you did all of this between 12.17 and 12.20, didn't you. Was that possible?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've given my answer to this, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you then agree with me if you say an indication of time, an indication of time would be -- if we, roughly speaking, said at 1.00 at 12.00 and 12.30, but if you said 12.17, this is no indication of time. This is time given in the most accurate way possible.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I really have answered -- this is given this way. But, I mean, it doesn't strike me as being a particular -- problematic point. This might have taken two minutes before or two minutes after.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. At any rate, this took three minutes, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. You're going on the timings that are written here, but it may not have taken three minutes to do. Maybe it took three and a half minutes, maybe it took five minutes, maybe it took six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come the next building was inspected at 12.20? Why is it we can't seem to agree on these things that seem totally simple and unequivocal, sir? This is obvious, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, have you found any that took -- take place exactly at the same time maybe? Maybe we saw a few buildings at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. One, two, three minutes, you walked around, if you had, and you noted this down, because there -- I can't possibly conceive of any other way for you to do this. If you look at 12-4, for example, you came there and you had sufficient time to measure the stain.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what this measures particularly, it measures the progression of the survey. It measures the progression of it. You're attaching importance to whether -- its minutiae exactly or not. It measures the progression from which building to which building to which building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you look at 12-6 now. This was -- this took six minutes to write, in view of the fact that the next one was done at 12.46. Well now this building at 12-6 is a building that obviously has two floors and an attic. You somehow managed to measure the hole in the roof. You look at the walls, and you give the exact description of the state of the walls. You enumerate the cracks on the second floor. You look at the corners of the roof and you even look at the adjacent buildings, giving accurate descriptions, noting all the details, and signing the report. And all it takes is six minutes, during which time you also have sufficient time to ascertain which projectiles were used, their calibre.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're just going around in circles. I'm going to repeat myself. Maybe this didn't take six minutes; maybe in fact it took 12 minutes to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So these entries are not accurate then?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're saying that these particular timings of when a visit was building -- sorry, a building was visited do not -- are not accurate. That's about the timings of visiting the building. These are approximate, but this is a damage survey. This is not about a -- racing around the town looking at -- looking at, in example, the chronometre in one's hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, that's precisely what worries me. You were supposed to determine the damage and not use three or four or five minutes to ascertain the damage when -- the time when the damage occurred, the type of weapon that caused the damage, the calibre of weapon that caused the damage, and count the damage that had been sustained by the roof and the interior of the house from the ground floor to the top-most floor. That were what you were supposed to do. Or else, what I can conclude is that your entries are not accurate, because the most precise data I can see in this report are the times given. Everything else seems to be more descriptive, but the time, at least, the timings should be beyond doubt.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports are descriptive and you will notice in the entries that there's usually quite a lot of information. I think that's what's very important, not these times in which the surveys were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. For example, tell me about 12-6. You took six minutes to do that. How were you able to ascertain the type of projectile? Do you remember this particular building at all? If not, please let us not waste anymore time.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this building, but I was looking at the type of damage that is indicated in this sheet. "Direct hit on the roof" is damage. The bearing structure of the roof, two wooden support beams. "House walls have been shaken up by the blast." I'm sorry, can I continue, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second direct hit has damaged the top of the house corner underneath the roof cornice. Now, we don't have any photographs here to see what that looks like. It looks to me -- it looks to me, that is its judgement made on the level and type of damage that would be carried out by this particular type of projectile. It's indicated second category, by the way, and normally there would be photographs to show the type of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you find any fragments of projectiles there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see, sir, any indication here that there are fragments of projectiles, but fragments of projectiles were identified by the teams. Sometimes I've given a very cursory look at this report, you will see indications like DVA Komada, which is two pieces, in which case the person who carried out the survey actually had the presence of mind: Yes, let's write down the pieces we found.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where it says clearly that projectiles were found, that's where projectiles were found. Wherever it doesn't state explicitly that projectiles were found, nothing was found, no fragments of projectiles. Am I reading you correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I didn't have an all-seeing eye on what was going on. You know I didn't carry out this survey. You know I wasn't looking at the teams. You know I'm not responsible for this work. I cannot say what each individual team was doing. We had originally asked them to identify projectiles and note down when they have found pieces, details of them. Now, it appears from my very cursory reading of this, a few times they did. But the problem is that we can't tell always when they did or if they were judging from fragments that they found, or if in fact they were judging on the type -- just simply on the basis of the type of damage and knowing that there was only a small number of different types of projectiles that were being used, which did create very different types of damage and would be recognised on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What we're looking at now, 12-6, Mr. Kaiser, allegedly you were the one who wrote this, that's at least what the document says?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about it as though someone else had actually written it. If you can look at the following page in B/C/S. There's no photograph there, as you said. If you look at the next page of the B/C/S version marked 725, last three digits.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I've found this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This photograph, does it have anything to do with the rest of the document or not? Do you know that? Or is it just difficult to say?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see a number written on this document, but I'm not quite sure -- near the caption. I'm not sure exactly to what that refers. Maybe it refers to number 6 entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we could please have a break now. I apologise, but I will need another 15 minutes to finish my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In view of the difficulties that the witness has experienced following these reports, I think we can allow you that 15 minutes, Mr. Petrovic. We will adjourn now for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, can we please briefly go back to Exhibit P63, tab 6. I would like to ask you -- I'm talking about the annex to your report. If you could please look at annex 1 to your report; it's a map. It's a sketch of the damage. Can I please ask you to put this map on the ELMO so that we can all follow. Can we please just zoom out a little so that we can see the entire image, because I can't see the image in its entirety on my monitor. If we can just zoom out, please. Zoom out. If we can just zoom the photograph out, please. Thank you. Mr. Kaiser, what I would ask you to do is the following: Can you look at this thick line down the middle. This line is probably a result of the photocopying process. If you can look just next to the thick line along the north wall of the Old Town, there are four or five impacts there, a group of four or five impacts. Can you see that? The north wall, a group of four or five impacts.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, the upper left corner around the Minceta Bastion, again the image is not very clear, but if we could just zoom out a little, I believe it would be possible to see what we are talking about. If we could make the image a bit smaller -- no, well then perhaps not. This copy's not good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Can we please show the witness my own copy of the map; it's the same map from Mr. Kaiser's report. Can we please have the image displayed in such a way to see the entirety of the Old Town. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Number 41 is the group of impacts to the north, number 41, and the group of six impacts. Then number 43 around the Minceta Bastion bears another group of five impacts. Next, near the Pile gate, which is the east wall, three impacts. And then at the far west, St. John's Bastion where we have six, eight, or possibly ten impacts. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation perhaps: Why were the impacts grouped in this way? Why are they -- are there groups of impacts in such a small space? The area marked as 41, number 43 around the Minceta Tower, the Pile gate, and St. John's Bastion.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of these impacts are outside -- they're outside of the walls, but to take a look at the impacts which are on the St. John's Tower, these impacts from the early period, of the October/November period, mainly this 82-millimetre rocket, we believed that there were groups of impacts because there would be -- these would be fired off in sequence at the same -- in the same general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you look at number 41, the impacts there, the north wall, those six impacts just outside the town walls, would you allow for the possibility, since they are grouped in this way and not scattered, that there may perhaps have been a target, something in this small area surrounding the number 41 that was being targeted specifically?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to remember where the car parking lot was. And I -- you see, these were -- we didn't examine these, but I remember that very close to the north wall there were cars parked and they had been damaged by -- they had been damaged by shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you about the grouping, the accumulation of impacts in such a small area. Might that not be a result of the fact that there was a target positioned there, otherwise the impacts would have been scattered all over this area if that had been a result of a random shooting?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I was referring to the way a certain weapon was simply used, this happened at a time when we weren't there. I mean, there may have been something there, I don't know. This was about October, November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you do allow for the possibility that if we look at how the impacts were grouped there was something there in the area that was a target for those who were firing?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring specifically to number 41?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: For example, specifically number 41 or number 43, just below the Minceta Tower or the Pile gate, because the grouping of the damage of the impact is very peculiar.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One of the witnesses mentioned that between the main road to the north of Dubrovnik, to the north of the north wall, there were positions of the town's defence. Is it perhaps possible that this group of impacts, number 41, was a result of activity between the forces that were deployed to the north of the town and beyond the main road, which is about 200 metres further north towards Mount Srdj?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I object to that question, Your Honours. Mr. Petrovic is putting a supposition or evidence of other witnesses, which this witness cannot possibly know or qualify, and ask him to draw a conclusion from substantive matters not within his own knowledge. Therefore I would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only wanted for the witness to say whether he allows for the possibility. I was not asking the witness to draw any specific conclusions. If we know that the defence forces were between the main road and the north wall, is it possible in the witness's opinion that these impacts that we're looking at were a result of activity by the defence forces? I'm not asking him to testify about this; I'm only asking whether he can allow for the possibility that this was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He certainly has been able to allow for the possibility that a grouping of points of impact could indicate that something was being targeted in the area and that perhaps is as much a matter of common sense as anything else. But what you're now asking seems to not only involve, as Mr. Kaufman says, the possibility of knowledge of other witnesses, but also requires a view about military operations, which seems not to be the field of Dr. Kaiser, if you will excuse me expressing that view, and is really something beyond his expertise or knowledge. And it will depend, I would suggest, on evidence of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, briefly can you look at annex 6 to your report, Exhibit P63, tab 6. Sir, can you please say when this preliminary financial -- plan was drawn up?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we were working on it on the spot, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was it completed?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was completed while we were still there, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you look at item D, please. There is something there that perhaps may assist us to determine the time, 17th of December, 1991, when the conversion was made between the dinars and the dollars. Is it on that date or around that date? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be around then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what was this report based on?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was based on a lot of supposition because we are putting in figures here on roof surfaces and things like that, it's based on numbers that are given locally for labour costs and material costs and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it based on the preliminary report compiled by the institute?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- it's not based on the preliminary report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this is a very general assessment which contains nothing specific or accurate about the assessment in terms of money?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very inaccurate, extremely inaccurate. This is one of the assignments that was sort of faxed out to the team in Dubrovnik, the things that it had to take care of immediately and then put back immediately, as soon as possible for the director-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another question, Your Honour. My apologies, but I hope I'm still within the time frame I promised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said recently, sir, that you heard that General Strugar had been indicted, didn't you? That's what you said yesterday in answer to one of my questions. When was it precisely that you heard this? Which year and which season, if you can tell us? Perhaps you may not be able to recollect the exact date, but perhaps you could give us the season or the year?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was probably when the indictment was issued, because the indictments are available on the Internet. And every so often I look at the Internet to see what documents -- what documents are there or if any decisions have been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This means it was probably in the autumn of 2001, since that's when the indictment was disclosed. I think that's beyond dispute.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been then. It might have even been later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask the usher's assistance. Can we show this document to the witness. Your Honours, it's the World Heritage newsletter for May and June 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, please, what sort of a journal is this? Are you familiar with this journal?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the different sectors and departments -- sectors of UNESCO, they have specific types of publications, and this is a publication of the World Heritage Centre of UNESCO, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 2 of this document, the first article on page 2. And the headline is: "Prevent crimes against culture." The section that begins: "Legal means." Paragraph 1, please. If you could have a look, sir. Can you please explain if the indictment for Dubrovnik was disclosed or unsealed on the 2nd of October, 2000, how can it be that the director-general of the institution we're talking about knows in May or June 2000 that the indictment exists? How is that possible for him to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: 2001 it's written here. On the newsletter at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 2001, yes. The indictment was published on the 2nd of October, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So I think there's a mistake in the question, the way it's been phrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my apologies. I think I said 2001, but obviously the translation was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the indictment was published on the 2nd of October, 2001, that much is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what you have in front of you is the World Heritage newsletter for May and June 2001, before the indictment was published. All I want to know is whether this witness can explain how that is possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't explain how that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does this perhaps have anything to do with your participation in this whole matter?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry? What does that mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does this have anything to do with your participation in the Dubrovnik problem since 1991 -- from 1991 to this very day?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have something to do with it. Dubrovnik's on the World Heritage List and there have been a whole bunch of UNESCO missions and a UNESCO rehabilitation plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this please be marked as a Defence exhibit, this document, unless there are any objections. And I have no further questions for this witness. I thank Mr. Kaiser for his patience over these days of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The World Heritage newsletter will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I'll attempt to be as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, you, I see, have brought with you to court a number of slides. Is that pursuant to the request that was made on the first day that you could perhaps obtain the best possible photographs which are appended to your report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in response to a request to retrieve photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So may we have those photographs?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on Day 27 of this trial, page 85 in the transcript at line 25 you were asked whether you had had any further contact with the federal authorities, other than that which you mentioned. You said no. Now, we know that Mr. Daniel Janicot accompanied you on earlier parts of your mission in answers you gave on cross-examination and in-chief.
