Do you know if Mr. Janicot had any further contact with these authorities?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. On day 28, page 16 at line 16, you talked about witnessing a Macedonian soldier putting on one side of the wall, putting a projectile whilst you were on the other side of the wall. I wonder if you could possibly elaborate on this matter, where exactly was that? Which wall are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about a street which is behind -- it's behind the Dominican Monastery, it's west of the Dominican Monastery, and this was carried out in -- this is in conjunction with the survey of the damage of October and November 1991. It took place in that framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: When we're talking about a wall, are we talking about the wall of the building or the wall of the old -- the ramparts of the Old Town, the walls of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the wall of a building, of a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: On day 28 at page 34 -- on page 37 you were questioned about what steps you took to report the presence of soldiers in the Old Town, namely those with the long-barrelled guns, as you mentioned. And Mr. Petrovic at page 37, line 13 of the protocol, read your statement to you, but he didn't complete the relevant paragraph that he was putting to you. And I would like to give you that opportunity now. You mentioned that you had seen very few of these soldiers. I would like to ask you what else you saw in the Old Town with respect to military hardware, equipment, units, whatever.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of the few soldiers that we saw, we didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you talked about something that you called a rocket mortar. You said it had fins. You gave a calibre estimate of something in the region of 82 millimetres. You said it was distinguishable from its more squat, 82-millimetre cousin. And you also said it was found in the tops of buildings, always on the same side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask Mr. Usher to place the table that has already been placed in front of you in examination-in-chief. This is contained in P51, MFI, in the very first pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Have a look, please, sir, at items 2 and 3, which you identified in-chief as the 82-millimetre items. Could you point out the rocket mortar, as you call it? Sorry, once again, sir --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you are pointing to item number 3. This is the item which you said had a flat trajectory?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And this is the item you found, as you say, at the tops of buildings, always on the same side. When you say "always on the same side," what do you mean, which side?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The east side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Which would be facing which direction geographically?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be facing backwards towards the hills of Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to submit this particular item as an exhibit. It was presented in-chief. I'm fully aware that at some later stage I'm going to have to make legal submissions as to the admissibility of P51, which is currently marked for identification. As I mentioned, this item was presented to Dr. Kaiser in-chief. Your Honours asked me if I wanted it introduced as an exhibit. It wasn't even marked for identification then. The same goes for a map of the walls of the Old Town, which my request also extends to, showing the impacts which was in fact presented to the witness in cross-examination by Mr. Petrovic. I should like at any rate for this item to be admitted as a separate exhibit. I have copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it could be collected by the court officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the same applies, as -- with respect to the walls of the Old Town, which was once again put to the witness in-chief, presented to the witness in cross-examination. I should like that to be tendered as an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the one, the numbers of which concludes 074?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the one with respect to the pieces of armament concludes 068?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Each of those will be received as an exhibit and given a separate and fresh number. They being part of that which is marked for identification as P51.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And as one last matter, Your Honour, there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll give them a number first, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first exhibit will be numbered Prosecution Exhibit P67 and the map of the Old Town will be numbered P68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And finally, a photograph that was presented to the witness in-chief which directly hinges on my next question. Perhaps this could be placed on the ELMO in front of the witness. This, one again, was a photograph which was presented to the witness in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, the photograph which is currently being placed on the display system for you we've been talking about rocket mortars. What do you see in that photograph? How would you describe that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see here the rear end of the cylinder with the little wings that have gone back into their resting position, stuck into the old port near the jetty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Is that your rocket mortar, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Could you -- I request that this would be submitted as an exhibit once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection to that, unless we clarify that this photograph does not relate to the month of December 1991. So with the proviso that these photograph is not dated December 1991, with that proviso, the Defence is ready to have this photograph admitted. If this can't be granted, then the matter becomes much more serious, which we may discuss now, if you like, Your Honours, or, by your leave, at a later date, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman, do you accept that this is not a photograph directly relating to the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, with the Court's leave I could ask the witness that particular question. And if he can't answer, then I'm quite happy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought we had an answer to it, but please do that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, are you able to tell us whether or not that particular projectile which you see in the photograph on the display machine, whether that relates to the 6th of December or an earlier date? Did you see it on one of your earlier tours?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said earlier, and I repeat, this is the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, who took this photograph? When was the photograph taken? How can we tell that this photograph is dated the 6th of December? Was the photograph taken by this witness? Where is this photograph, the original of this photograph? Are we going to open all these questions now? In that case, I beg to be allowed to ask these questions. Based on what the witness was doing himself, he remembers nothing. He vaguely remembers this photograph, but it's not exactly clear when and where this photograph was taken. Therefore, Your Honours, I object to this photograph being admitted as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman, do you plan to explore any of those issues in your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can put the report in front of Dr. Kaiser himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, if you could take P51 MFI, let us turn to the damage report itself. Just so that I don't get accused of completely leading you on that matter, it's to be found in the first volume at 01069129 Z40, but, sir, before you look at that particular page -- have it in front of you but don't look at the page. As far as the methodology was concerned the photographs which are appended to the damage survey reports, were they photographed at the same time of the compilation of the survey of that particular site at a later date, or at an earlier date

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be made at the time of the survey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Fine. So please open up the bundle at Z40. In the B/C/S version it's 9129. I believe you have the English version open in front of you, sir. Please tell the Court the date of the preparation of this particular site, survey.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was prepared on the 10th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And the date that appears there as the date of the impact as it were?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that that should clear the matter up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I propose, Mr. Petrovic, to admit the exhibit on the basis of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. The witness who has testified before you for these last few days, the reports that he purportedly drew up himself, this witness is unable to comment on these reports. He remembers neither what this is nor where this is. At Z40, we have a report drawn up by Paula Kolic and Ivica Zile. The witness assumes responsibility to confirm that this photograph is indeed linked to that report. How? Based on what, Your Honours? He doesn't even know where he purports to have been when he drew up the report. How can we possibly have an exhibit like this admitted under the circumstances, there being no indication between any link between the witness and Z40. That is the first matter. Secondly, Your Honours, if you look at the text of Z40, if you look at the text, where can you find that in the text? Where can you find a description of what we can see in the photograph and who is behind it? There is simply no link between the two. I am honestly surprised that Mr. Kaiser is able to confirm that the photograph was taken on the 6th of December, if we have seen that he is not exactly familiar with 30-something buildings that have his name signed under them. So then please, Your Honours, at the very least, may I be allowed to ask questions about this photograph. I think, however, that this would be superfluous. Time as of value and I would only be forced more and more time on this matter, if allowed to re-direct. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. No, you will not be allowed to ask further questions, but I will. Dr. Kaiser, what is your basis of knowledge for your evidence that this was a photograph taken in respect of the damage on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the 7th and the 8th of December, we divided the town into two parts. I went around with Mr. Franic and we carried out a very quick survey. This is not like a Garista or Varicevo or places like that. This is a very obvious place. I kind of remember this place. This is the port. And I remember crossing along in front and seeing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there anything further, Mr. Kaufman, you want to ask about this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: No. And I thank Your Honour for clarifying the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The ruling which I gave, Mr. Petrovic, stands, the document will be received as an exhibit in view of the personal memory of the testify witness. But you can be assured that the matters that you have mentioned will be very much exercising the mind of the Chamber as it comes to weigh the reliance it can place on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P69 and may I request copies for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, briefly moving on. I would like to remind you of some things that you said in cross-examination. Now, Day 28, page 61, line 10, you stated that: The damage of October and November had already been identified, is that correct, identified by the institute when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And the first task you had was to verify that damage?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And such you did as is evidenced by annex 3 to your report at P63, tab 6?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by annex 3 and also by 12 pages in the body of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, you state at page 72 of Day 28, line 17, that you prepared your report for the director-general of UNESCO and you did so with accuracy and conscientiously. Is that still the case?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So Mr. Petrovic, in cross-examination, put a whole string of buildings to you, which appear in annex 3 to your report. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the comparison between the annex 3 and the large report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And the institute's report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the institute's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: He then purported to show you the same buildings as they appeared in the institute's report. Now, Mr. Petrovic was firing these various items at you at a pretty high-speed. Are you sure that you read the details of all these items in detail, from the institute report as they were being put to you in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, we can do this in a time-consuming way by going over all those items one by one and allowing you to give your comment on each and every one of them, or I can ask you in a shorthand way whether or not you managed to notice whether there was corresponding features between what Mr. Petrovic was putting to you as having been noted by you in your report and what was noted by the institute in their report.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you remember, there were not very long discussions about this and not long views of these documents. But I remember the first day that the Defence counsel started to do this, he did -- there was -- we spent some time on Ulica Boskoviceva. It was clear on the discussion of the console, the balustrade, the balcony, that there was an overlap, if that's what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, there might have been an overlap, sir, but I have been over those particular buildings last night as they were put to you, and I want to ask you whether you remember whether there was an exact correlation between the items that you said had incurred damage in October and November in annex 3 to your report and the identification of the damage as it appeared in the institute's report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Let me take, for example, annex 3, item 26, the house at Siroka Street 5. There in annex 3 is your report, if you would like to have -- that's open in front of you. There in your report you talk about second floor consul -- cornice damaged by shrapnel and facade, superficial damage. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And you add: "The roof seems to have been hit by mortar on the 6th of December. Needs to be thoroughly examined."

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, that same item was put to you as having been reported at insula 11, number 36. Do you remember how that damage was described there and whether there was any correlation between the damage that you talked about and the damage that was identified by the institute?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't have time to read the entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to read the entry?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to it. It's to be found in volume 2 of the English version, item number 11 -- insula 11, item 36. You were questioned on this. You were asked merely to give the date of the preparation of the report; you were not asked to go into details. But now I give --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I ask you, sir, if what you reported in October and November is what is reported on December 6th.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I will look at both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Certainly. Do you have an answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And your answer?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of December this building was gutted by flame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And in October and November?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had very superficial damage done to the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do I understand from that answer, sir -- we can go through other buildings because I can give you plenty of examples. The documents eventually, I hope, will be before Your Honours so that we can do the distinctions as is necessary but, can I understand from you, sir, that it is possible to do a filtering exercise, that you can take the document, the institute's report which purports to portray the damage of December the 6th and you can filter out the damage having occurred in October and November, if necessary, by taking your annex 3 and subtracting that from the institute's report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is laborious but it is very easy to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Well, I won't trouble you anymore with that. I don't want to take up too much of your time. Let us move quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I pause -- ask you to pause to make the observation that I hope you're not expecting the Chamber to do that laborious task?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't have the skill nor the knowledge, nor do we want to spend the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't intending on doing that. And Your Honours will hear when I make my submissions on the matter, I submit and I will submit that this document P51 which is currently marked for identification is admissible and of course the weight has been challenged and challenged very competently, I must say, by Mr. Petrovic, although I believe it has substantial weight and that weight I will argue in front of the Chamber. However, this document is admissible. If necessary, Mr. Petrovic and I will of course engage in conversations to make the Chamber's life easy in respect of this matter. But admissibility is a separate issue from weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're not dealing with the question of admissibility, Mr. Petrovic, don't worry --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is an alternative. I could explore, if necessary, the possibility of requesting very kindly, of course, from Dr. Kaiser himself who is a very eager individual, I know from my personal contact with him, although I don't wish to labour him and burden him unnecessarily, of course, I would have to speak to him about this matter asking him for his assistance in this matter. But I fear that should not really be necessary. I feel that Mr. Petrovic and I could possibly reach some other agreement, albeit at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We look forward to that. Filing that, could I indicate tat were you to move at a later time for leave to recall Dr. Kaiser, that would probably be for the purpose of giving the product of this effort. That would be considered by the Chamber. I think it would be an enormous waste of time of everybody to attempt to do that as a matter of re-examination at the present time. And -- though we can leave it on that basis, as long as you are conscious of the Chamber's concern that left as it is the position would be considered to be quite unsatisfactory to the point of view of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fully conscious of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, final questions, you'll be pleased to know. If you could open up once again P63, tab 6, that's your report, the English version. Mr. Petrovic questioned you on paragraph C.2.1 of that report. And the general thrust of his questions in this matter were on matters of possible political propaganda. The sentence that was put to you was that the reports' assessments are well drafted but often provide nothing more than the impression, and you were cross-examined on what was meant by an impression. I would like to take you to the end of that particular section of your report and ask you to read out the very last photograph of that particular section, which perhaps elaborates your views of the institute's methodology and reports.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the ending -- the ending -- last paragraph on that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: No, on the next page, 03073347. The last paragraph at the section. Please, sir.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That said, the document's very considerable worth must also be highlighted. It pinpoints the damage accurately ad puts forward conclusions which are generally restrained and consistently incontrovertible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, that is the institute's report for October and November. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You have already told the Court that you were the person who instituted the methodology and instituted the classification, set the team members out on their specific tasks. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that they carried out their tasks in the same way that they carried out their tasks in October and November?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm satisfied that they carried out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, we know that you had various reasons to qualify the institute's tasks, and you set that out as a result of their not being ballistic's experts and sometimes, in your opinion, misdiagnosing, if I could say, the calibre of the projectile which caused the damage which they viewed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: That was your reservation?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yet, in C.2.1 when you're talking about the methodology and how the institute carried out their work, you say that their assessment of damage is accurate. Is that correct, sir? You just read out the passage.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe that their work on the report of the 6th of December, the later report, the report that is now P51 MFI, that their work on that report would have been any different from their work on the October and November report, since you were the person who instituted that methodology, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that we worked with for October and November I would fully expect that they would continue on, they would carry on the proper methodology and assessment that we carried out together with them in October and November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, in your report you incorporated annex 7. Annex 7 is a list of statistics, is it not --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: -- Which was provided to you by the institute for the protection of monuments?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You incorporated annex 7 into the main body of your report, did you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I incorporated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You furthermore attached maps from the institute, 4A and 4B, or B in particular --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: As a map being prepared after the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report you gave to the director-general of UNESCO, is it not?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And you have already said that your mandate to the director of UNESCO was to accurately report what you had witnessed in Dubrovnik, the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I take it, sir, you wouldn't incorporate something in your report that you didn't think was reliable, would you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regarded this document, these maps, as very credible -- although a work in progress. But they were very credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise for the time that you've had to spend on the witness stand, but I do thank you ever so much for coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you have any questions of the witness before he descends from the witness stand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, doctor, the time has been extensive, but I think necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please turn the microphone on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I do apologise. I thank you for your attendance. The time has been lengthy, but I think necessary. I'm delighted to say that you are now excused and free to go. Mr. Kaufman, the photographs that were mentioned, are you proposing to do something with those?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall of course make sure that these are the photographs which are the photographs appended to Dr. Kaiser's report, and once I have gone through that exercise I will submit them to the Trial Chamber. I believe that there is already an agreement that they do be tendered, and I hope that can be done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think all of us would be grateful for a better quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if these are photographs which were appended to the annex which we received in somewhat better form on Friday, if these are those photographs, this is quite okay as far as the Defence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is another witness waiting outside. I have substantial legal argument to make on the matter of asking P51 to be tendered as an exhibit. I wonder whether Your Honours want to hear that legal argument now or at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you say "extensive," can you put an estimate in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, not so extensive. I meant 10 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. The witness will take how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Re is going to be handling the next witness. I believe he indicated it was something in the region of three quarters of an hour. Am I correct, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that evidence in-chief or the whole process?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps instead of speaking on Mr. Re's behalf I can let it come from the horse's mouth, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. I anticipate, I would hope to be through his evidence in 45 minutes to an hour or so. I'm told from Mr. Rodic that he doesn't think he'd be more than 2 hours. Prosecution has some concerns that it may actually take that long with the witness who is here for proof of death, a forensic pathologist; however I do note that he has been in The Hague since Saturday. We'd be quite anxious to get him on and completed today if we possibly could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There will be no way if you're going to take possibly an hour, that even with a limited cross-examination of a similar duration that he could finish today. If you look at the time now, we have just over an hour sitting time remaining today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That must have been supreme optimism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And I notice there is a special time requirement for a witness to be recalled tomorrow, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A witness who must finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's Ambassador Alajbeg. Perhaps if the -- my discussions with Ms. Lamb - I'll be here tomorrow - indicate that the Prosecution on present indications only has about five to ten minutes of re-examination on present cross-examination. Perhaps if my learned friends could indicate how long they expect to be -- to continue their cross-examination, we might be able to better plan -- the two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. -- I thought we were going to get a duet. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, it wouldn't be at all that pleasant, Your Honour. Thank you. As regards the witness Alajbeg. Can we please start tomorrow morning with Mrs. Alajbeg. We shall certainly complete our part tomorrow, but I would like to ask you that we do not start with Mr. Ciganovic tonight, or perhaps if we do start -- if we do start, let us start with her Madam Alajbeg tomorrow so that -- tomorrow afternoon so that we will make sure that she will make certain that she will finish testifying tomorrow and can leave tomorrow. So if we start at the beginning of tomorrow's sittings, so then we can be quite certain that she will have completed her testifying, as far as the Defence is concerned, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The position would appear to be that if we put to one side for the moment legal argument, it would be possible to conclude the evidence in-chief of the witness that is waiting today. Just whether it would be possible to conclude cross-examination late tomorrow is somewhat uncertain and it could well be that the witness's evidence would not be concluded until Friday. I can't see any way of overcoming that at the moment. I think the most practical course - returning to Mr. Kaufman - would be to defer the question of legal argument until we have 20 minutes to half an hour to spare on -- in the course of tomorrow or Friday for that. And in the meantime, after the break, to hear the evidence in-chief of the witness with cross-examination not to be concluded today, and that cross-examination will be taken up after we have finished with the evidence of the Ambassador who is to be recalled first thing tomorrow morning. Is that convenient to all parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being so, I think we will have the break now, and then we can get straight into the evidence of the waiting witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you like to take the affirmation that will now be shown to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Dr. Ciganovic, can you please give the Chamber your full name and occupation.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: My full name is Djordje Ciganovic. My occupation is pathologist and cytologist and forensic medicine specialist. So I'm a physician, a specialist.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that at the Pancevo health or medical centre which is located near Belgrade in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm currently working at the Pancevo health centre which is near Belgrade in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about your medical qualifications. You have a medical agree. When did you graduate from medical school and which medical school was it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated in 1973 from the medical faculty in Zagreb, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you work after your graduation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: After my graduation I worked in Dubrovnik as a general practitioner until the year 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you work at the Dubrovnik general hospital or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I worked at the medical centre in Dubrovnik until that time. After that, I went for my specialisation, specialised studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you do your specialised studies, for how long, and what was the specialisation, or the degree or qualification you obtained?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: From 1979 to 1983 I pursued my specialisation in the field of pathology at the medical faculty in Zagreb. And in parallel with that, I also graduated -- I actually finished my post-graduate studies in the field of medical cytology and obtained my master's degree in the field of pathology. After this, I also completed my specialised studies in the area of cytology, and after that my specialised studies in the forensic medicine field, which I completed in 1987. From 1983 I worked as the chief of the pathology and cytology and forensic medicine service in Dubrovnik and also -- I did work in all these mentioned fields. My specialisation, my specialised degree, in forensic medicine and cytology was something which evolved in parallel with my work in Dubrovnik until the year 1987 [Realtime transcript read in error "1997"], that is to say my studies in those fields evolved in parallel. And I had to travel -- to commute several times a week between Dubrovnik and Zagreb in order to perform my duties in both these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The transcript says you said 1997. Did you say 1997 or 1987, the commuting between Dubrovnik and Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: From 1983 to 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Until when were you the chief pathologist or the chief of pathology at Dubrovnik general hospital?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: This was until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you leave Dubrovnik for Pancevo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I left at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did your duties as the chief of pathology at Dubrovnik general hospital until the end of 1992 involve? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I did work in the field of pathology, namely clinical autopsies, histopathological analyses for diagnostic purposes on live patients, as well as psychological tests or analyses on live patients for the purpose of establishing diagnosis. Apart from that, I also worked in the forensic medicine field, namely I undertook forensic medicine autopsies and forensic medicine expertise. And I rendered such forensic expertise and expert opinions in court in the case of bodily harm and injury in criminal cases as well as in litigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Chamber as an estimate how many autopsies you would have performed at Dubrovnik between 1983 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: In this period I undertook court autopsies in Dubrovnik, all of them, all of them -- all of the necessary autopsies for the court. And on average there would be 70 of them per year. In addition to that, for four years I also, in parallel with pursuing my other specialised studies, I also undertook other court autopsies at the forensic medicine institute in Zagreb during my specialised studies, where all of us were pursuing specialised studies would work together on all the necessary post-mortems. And there were about seven on -- about seven autopsies was the daily average. So if I were to add up all the forensic medical autopsies that I had done together collectively with my colleagues and those which I undertook myself, the number that I would obtain would be about 8.000, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did each of these autopsies -- a moment ago you mentioned court appearances, did each of these autopsies involve your attending court with an investigating judge or magistrate?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Each of these forensic autopsies necessitated my appearance before the investigating judge. And as often as not, later, also in criminal proceedings, before regular courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you prepare or have prepared documents for the investigating judge and your appearances in court?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I would, as a rule, provide my finding and my opinion in writing in such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you in Dubrovnik in the period September to December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your main duty in that period?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period my main duty was to examine the people who were -- who had been killed during the war which had taken place there, in that period. My other duties had been reduced to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you perform your duty of examining people who had been killed in the war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I performed these examinations in the ward, the pathology -- the pathology, cytology, and forensic medicine ward of the medical centre in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which hospital?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: That is the general hospital in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was that located outside of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: It was located -- is located outside the Old Town, but quite nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And could you estimate for the Trial Chamber approximately how many autopsies you performed on what you've described as the victims of war in that period, September to December -- or to mid-December 1991.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall with precision, but I believe the number exceeded 100 autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to describe for the Trial Chamber the conditions under which you were working at the hospital in performing these autopsies during that period.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: In the period in question in Dubrovnik, there was no electricity, there was no water, and there was no heating. So the same conditions also obtained in the hospital, apart from the fact that occasionally we had current provided by -- electricity provided by the generator.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you -- you were born in 1951. Were you mobilised during 1991 or did you have a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not mobilised in the period from September to December 1991, because my wartime duty station within the civilian service was precisely to perform the duties which I did perform during this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you receive a written notification of your war obligation or your wartime duty station, or was it something that was understood by you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes to which one? Yes, it was understood by you or yes you received something in writing?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out, all who were -- all men who were fit, able for work, were assigned their wartime duties stations or stations in the civilian service, given the extraordinary circumstances. So it was also -- everybody in the hospital was assigned a specific duty along those lines, and I was assigned to this particular position that I described for you, which I actually held throughout the war. And of course it was also my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And just on this topic of military service or mobilisation, did you do JNA service? If so, when?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I did my military service with the JNA in 1976. And after completing my military service, in my service booklet I was assigned a station for the future, namely my assignment was in the civilian service in the event of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you living in September, October, November, and December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was living in Dubrovnik in that period at three different addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you ever living in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: One of these places was, yes, in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you experience shelling in that period, September, October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can you tell the Trial Chamber about your experience of shelling over that period?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Shelling was very frequent. In fact, it was a daily occurrence practically. It took place mostly during the day. And as a rule, it would last for a number of hours. Namely, it had a beginning and an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you living or staying on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, I was living in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And on which street were you living?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: The name of the street is Kneza Hrvasa. This is a small street behind the cathedral in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And why were you in that place?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was there because my grandfather has a flat in this street and that is why I stayed there, believing that I would be safer in the Old Town than outside it from the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you think you would be safer in the Old Town than outside?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought that because until that time we -- the Old Town came under less shelling and the areas outside the Old Town came under heavier shelling. Apart from that, I would -- I had to go to the hospital at least once daily and sometimes many more times than that to do my work there. And then to return home on foot. Because there was no petrol, one could not drive one's car. This was, in fact, the shortest route that I could take in order to make this trip to work and back as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there shelling on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can you say about the shelling on that day relative to the shelling you had experienced over the previous few months?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: On that particular day, the Old Town came under considerable shelling and I was in the cellar of the house in which I lived. After the shelling I went outside, together with the other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll come to that in a moment. The first question I wish to explore with you is: How would you describe the shelling on that day in comparison to the shelling that you had experienced in Dubrovnik over the preceding few months? I mean, how would you describe the intensity of it on that day?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: The shelling that day was quite intense, but even before that I had experienced shelling of considerable intensity while I had been living in my house outside the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was your house outside the town, in what street?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: My house outside the town was in a street which was called the Put of the JNA at that time and its current name is Put Andrije Hebranga. And this is the a circular road that leads to the Old Town and outside the Old Town. It is immediately above the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any particular days in the months preceding the 6th of December that stand out in your mind as when there had been particularly intense shelling?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were days, but now I cannot recall which days those were. Because of the intensity of the shelling, I moved out of my house because it was very dangerous there. I moved to another section of town, the section of town called Lapad, and stayed with friends there. In fact, they had a shelter. Sometime later when it became dangerous there as well, I moved into the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you were telling the Chamber about the 6th of December. And you said "the Old Town came under considerable shelling and you were in the cellar of your house which you lived after the shelling and went outside, together with some other people. About what time did the shelling start on that day?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly, but I believe it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the cellar for, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I remained for quite many hours, but I can't remember exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can you say about damage that you may have observed after you went outside?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: When I went outside I noticed substantial damage. There were fragments of shells, windows that had been shattered, and doors, too. Several buildings in the Old Town were ablaze. And everything looked quite untidy and damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did that compare to the Old Town on the 5th of December, 1991, that is the damage you saw on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, there had been no such damage in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your building damaged on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: My building was never hit directly during this war, but it was damaged both on the 6th of December and in previous -- during previous shelling. It was damaged by shrapnel. About 50 shells landed near my house throughout the war at a distance of between 3 and 10 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In case there's any confusion, I'm -- hopefully I'm directing you to the building you were staying in on the 6th of December, as opposed to your house outside the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I misunderstood the question. On the 6th of December, not a single shell landed near the house in which I was staying in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Doing your best, can you please tell the Trial Chamber what buildings you saw, what specific buildings you saw damaged or on fire in the Old Town on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: A building was on fire where the headquarters of the summer festival were, the Dubrovnik summer festival. It's on old building which is a protected monument. These protected monuments are usually referred to as palaces. Also, two other buildings on Od Puca street, which is a small tree -- street parallel to the Stradun near the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you -- in the last part of your answer, did you mean those buildings were on fire?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Those buildings were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've told us about fire damage. What about other damage or damage to other buildings that fell short of buildings being on fire? I appreciate it's been a long time, but doing your best can you please tell the Trial Chamber about the damage to any specific buildings you can remember.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Many roofs had been hit by shells and the resulting damage was substantial. Many shells landed on the ground so you could see craters resulting from explosions and you could see shrapnel causing damage to the surrounding houses and walls. Also, architectural ornament was damaged on many buildings and on many monuments inside the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At a general description, Dr. Ciganovic, is there any way you can more specific about any specific buildings you can remember damage to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be more specific because almost every building had sustained at least some damage from shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you go to work on the 6th of December after you left the cellar of the building you were staying in?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to work once the shelling was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the next day, the 7th of December, 1991? Did you go to work in your job performing autopsies in the general hospital in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you perform a number of autopsies on that day, that's the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I performed 19 autopsies, partial autopsies, on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you prepare a report of the 19 autopsies on that day?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I prepared a report on the autopsies that I performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you a document dated the 7th of December, 1991. The first thing I want to you to do, doctor, is just to identify whether that is in fact a report relating to those 19 autopsies on the 7th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You told the Chamber earlier about the general conditions under which you performed autopsies in late 1991. Now, I want you to tell the Trial Chamber in more detail as to the procedures you generally employed when a body was brought to the hospital in that period.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period and on that particular day, the procedure I followed was to establish the identity of the victim, to ascertain what caused the death and how the death came about. I mainly used external examination of the body with partial autopsy, which implies opening those parts of the body which had sustained damage in order to ascertain with any degree of certainty what the cause of death had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I'll go into that in a little bit more detail in a moment. But first, how many people were present -- or, sorry. I'll withdraw that part. The body came to the hospital. Where was the body taken to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: The body came to the hospital, and it was taken straight to the morgue at the section room of the pathology and forensic medicine ward at the hospital. After the autopsy, the body's buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the morgue a separate room to the autopsy room?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have assistance in performing -- assistants, not assistance, in performing the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I did have an assistant for performing autopsies. This is common in my line of work. There was another autopsy assistant who had been mobilised to work with the ambulance as a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have assistants, that's with a T, when you performed your autopsies on the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 7th of December the autopsy assistant was with me, Drago Kaleb was the name. He was also an employee of the general hospital in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who else was present when you performed your autopsies on that day?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, as in all other cases, the investigating judge of the district court in Dubrovnik was there, the crime technician of the Dubrovnik police --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I object to this way of examining a witness. The witness has been shown a document to identify, and he did identify the document. But it is not proper for the witness when answering the questions of my learned friend and colleague to read the document and then provide his answers based on reading the document. He should tell us based on his memory who was there on the 7th of December. That's what the question was about. For him to tell us based on his recollection who was there on the 7th of December. Or perhaps the question should be: Can you, sir, please read out who was with you on the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In my submission it comes to the same point. I didn't understand this to be a memory test in relation to who was with him on the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the point is taken. If this is the doctor's own report and if it was prepared at about that time, he may properly be able to refresh his memory. But be conscious of the objection, if you would, and try and avoid the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Dr. Ciganovic, can you recall, without looking at your report, who was present in the autopsies you performed on the 7th of December, 1991. That's a yes or no question -- answer.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can recall the positions of the people who were present, because the autopsy -- forensic autopsy is always performed in the same way. I remember specifically by name my assistant, Drago Kaleb, and the investigating judge, Miloglav. I don't remember any other persons present.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said you don't remember any other persons present. You've identified the report as a report which prepared for the autopsies on that day, which is your report. Are the names of the other people whose names you can't recall in that document, without looking at it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall the names of the other people. I know that there was a crime technician, a crime inspector, a recording clerk, an investigating judge, my assistant, and myself. And there was another person who is a medical worker and who was appointed in the course of the war as the commander of the identification platoon. By name, Dr. Raguz.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would looking at the report in front of you refresh your memory as to the names of all people present? That's without looking at it, doctor.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Without looking?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. If you looked at the document, would it refresh your memory as to the names of the people present? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: If I could look at the document, I would recall the people because those were people that I had also worked with in peacetime, performing the same tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: With the Chamber's leave, could the witness be allowed to refresh his memory from his report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell me, this report is your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you tell me when it was prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was prepared on the 7th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He may refresh his memory, Mr. Re, if the report is able to assist him in that way, by looking at the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You understand, doctor?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you look at the report. If there are any names that you haven't mentioned so far that you have forgotten, could you please tell the Trial Chamber who else was present.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: The police inspector, Damira Poljanic; crime technicians of the Dubrovnik police, Matija Rebric and Ivica Stankovic. I knew all these people personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. A short while ago you were telling the Trial Chamber about the procedures you employed, and you got up to where you said you performed a partial examination or a -- I'm sorry, I've lost the transcript and I can't remember the exact words that the witness used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "A partial autopsy", the doctor said, are following physical examination, the autopsies being -- the partial autopsy being to damaged or injured parts of the body. I think that was the effect of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you actually do? What did your partial autopsy actually involve? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: After examining the entire body - I'm referring to the external examination - after examining the clothes, the skin, and any other external marks of injury, I would proceed to examine the depth of the injury in order to determine the channel and the depth of the wound, the direction of the channel, and the intensity of the damage sustained by the internal organs. And also, to reach, if I could, the object that caused the injury, which more often than not was lodged inside the victim's body. This entailed partially opening parts of the body, specific parts of the body, where the injury occurred so that I could get inside by using my instruments and have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In what circumstances did you perform a full internal autopsy or examination?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Full autopsies would be performed in cases where I could not ascertain the cause of death, as described.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you record what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I dictated to a court recording clerk who was in the adjacent room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the accused has just made a complaint to me -- well, that -- it was nothing after all, Your Honours. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's all right. Thank you. It seems to be all right now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, there's no problem at all. Several days ago I told you - at least according to the instructions I received from my doctor - this is a spine problem when I hold my head up. There's some sort of interruption that causes me to cough, you see, and that's why I try to lower my head, have some tea, to stop this so then I feel better. That's what this was about. But other than that, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry we interrupted you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your answer was you dictated to a court recording clerk who was in an adjacent room. Did anyone take notes at the time you were performing your external, or partial internal examination or internal examination?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I kept notes whenever I found something. And following each examination, I would go to the adjacent room and dictate my notes to the recording clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you keep the notes on?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I kept notes on ordinary paper, and I used a pen to take them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your practice in relation to those notes in compiling the report and what you did with those notes?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: When performing a forensic autopsy, I had been trained to memorise everything that I saw and found. And after that, to dictate into a tape recorder or to a recording clerk my findings and my opinion. In these specific cases, as there were quite a number of bodies there, I made notes, noting only the essential information on a piece of paper. After that, I would dictate everything that I had found to the recording clerk, after which the notes would usually be thrown away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you still have the notes that you made of these particular 19 autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have the notes that I made in the autopsy -- in the autopsy room. The pen itself was blood smeared because my hands were covered in blood and the paper, too, was blood stained. So the lot was discarded after the autopsy was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The front page of the report from which you've refreshed your memory refers to six people as present during the examination. The first is the investigating judge Pero Miloglav. What was his role?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the investigating judge who carried out an investigation on behalf of the court. In this case, the reason was that people had been killed and that people had sustained bodily harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just turn to the final page of the report. There's a signature on it. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whose signature it is.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of this report, you can't see a clear signature there but my name was typed up as well as the name of the investigating judge. In all cases where autopsies are carried out, the reports are signed by myself and the investigating judge, which is the case with this document, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that the English translation does not correspond with the B/C/S document in its entirety. Under the names we see autopsy carried out by Dr. Djordje Ciganovic in the presence of the investigating judge, Pero Miloglav. In the English version there's an additional clarification concerning the stamp, Dubrovnik district court, Republic of Croatia. And to the left there is the following text: An employee of this court Ane Glavanic certifying that this corresponds with the original. But this seems to be the only person who actually personally signed this document, which means neither the investigating judge nor the doctor who performed the autopsy put their signatures there, and this particular section of the text that I've just read out to you seems not to have been translated into English, in the English version of the document. So this is something we believe you need to take into account. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was just about in fact to explore that with the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Dr. Ciganovic, if you look in the screen -- look at the screen in front of you, you will see the -- that portion which Mr. Rodic just referred to has been enlarged. Now, can you see the signature there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: This signature belongs to an employee of the district -- Dubrovnik district court administration. They made the photocopies and they put a seal on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So are you telling the Trial Chamber that this is a copy -- a certified copy issued by the Dubrovnik court rather than the original of the report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I would identify this document. It's a certified document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was your practice and that of the investigating judge in relation to signing the original, and where did it go?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: This report was copied at least three times, three separate copies were made. The investigating judge and myself signed it -- signed at least one of the copies. While the remaining copies, because of the needs of the court, were sent to different places. All the copies were forwarded to the court and should be in the court's archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The report refers to 19 autopsies you performed on the 6th of -- sorry, the 7th of December, 1991. Are you able now, some 12 and a bit years after -- sorry, 13 -- 12 and a bit years afterwards able to remember the names or the details of the autopsies you performed on that day?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall all the names of those that had been killed on that day, with the exception of one person, namely Pavo Urban who was a photographer, a photojournalist, and quite a well-known person in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are the details of your autopsy on Pavo Urban in that report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could turn to the fifteenth autopsy you performed.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the autopsy I performed on Pavo Urban's body.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And are the details of the autopsy you performed accurately recorded in that report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: The details of this autopsy are indeed accurately recorded in this report. Furthermore, there is a typo that was made and corrected, by hand, that was made at the time, on the 7th of December, 1991, in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think that -- that hasn't come out in the English. What is the typographical error you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Where there is the description of the autopsy, line 5, it says: "In the area of the hip." And then this was crossed out and the word "naval" was added in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting or someone else's?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe this is my handwriting, but I can't remember whether I made this correction or whether the correction was inserted by the recording clerk once the document had been typed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is a yes or no question. Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber about the details of the autopsy you performed on Pavo Urban without referring to your autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that he had one injury in the naval area, an explosive wound on the surface of the skin, which was several centimetres in diametre, 5 or 6 centimetres, I believe it was, through which one could see the damaged intestines and other abdominal organs, wells the profuse bleeding inside the abdominal cavity, as well as the signs of blood flowing from the wound across the surrounding skin. Inside the abdomen I found a fragment of the explosive device that had caused the damage and haemorrhage was the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just referred to an explosive device causing damage and haemorrhage being the cause of death. How were you able to diagnose the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the signs of haemorrhage of -- on the corpse. A corpse which had bled to death has characteristic signs which are, of course, easily observable by physicians, specialists of my profile. This is clear evidence that the person in question bled to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You first referred to seeing in the naval area an explosive wound. Can you put it -- can you please tell the Trial Chamber in lay terms what an explosive wound is or describe an explosive wound and how you're able to say that the wound you saw was an explosive wound.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was familiar with such types of wounds also from my earlier practice, namely explosive wounds have identifiable characteristics. First of all, an irregular and, as a rule, large entry opening with an irregular wound on the skin which features contused and torn edges. And this contused edge of the wound, which is caused by the entry of a projectile into the body, if the wound was inflicted by a nearby explosion, at close range that is, there is also a sign of burning on the edges and around the edges of the wound; while inside the wound -- at the entry and inside the wound there is also a trace of the passage of the projectile which is caused by the dust and the specks from the surface of the projectile. Inside the body, there is very heavy damage which is observable with a wide channel, around which channel there is an area which is an area where the tissue is contused due to the transfer of the kinetic energy of the projectile to the soft tissues of the organism. The explosive device or projectile is, as a rule, inside the body, because due to its irregular shape it does not have a large penetrating capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does it differ from a gunshot wound, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: It differs very much from a wound inflicted by a firearm, such as a pistol or a rifle or something similar to that, because the bullet of a firearm mainly causes a regular round entry, aperture. It has a more regularly-shaped channel of the passage of the bullet through the body, and as a rule it exits the body through an exit wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from the irregularity of the wounds and the other things you have just described which enable you to distinguish an explosive injury, what other signs do you find on the bodies of people who have suffered different types of explosive injuries?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: If the wound was inflicted by an explosion from close range, as a rule, there are a number of explosive wounds. If the explosion was from a farther distance, there is a smaller number of wounds and sometimes just one explosive wound. Some of these explosive wounds are just like small lacerations on the body's skin, while some of the -- some are of -- some cover a larger surface. And if there are a number of such wounds, they are all -- they all differ in size.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about an injury from, say, ricochetting shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: From -- a wound from a ricochetting shrapnel, if the shrapnel is what you mean, yes, it looks just exactly like a directly inflicted wound but it is of a lesser intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were photographs taken of the bodies upon which you performed those 19 autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was customary when performing forensic autopsies for the crime technician to take photographs of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you please show the witness a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you can turn to your report, does your report and body number 15 which you've identified as Pavo Urban, does that refer to a photograph and a number?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What number is that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that number 15 in the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It has a photo number 74 next to it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: This number is there because that is the 74th victims of the total number of victims since the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can you tell the Trial Chamber about the photograph which is in front -- which is in front of you on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: On the photograph we can see a partially unclad dead body with a bodily injury in the naval area. It is -- the photograph is of rather poor quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it the photograph -- is it a photograph of Pavo Urban taken at the time you performed your autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may clarify. All these photographs were made prior to the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You referred earlier to an explosive injury about 5 centimetres in diametre. Can you see that -- is that particular injury depicted on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your opinion as to the cause of that particular injury?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC
utterances.text: All the characteristics of the wound on the surface inside the body were -- and inside the body were the characteristics of an injury inflicted by an explosion and from the abdomen near the spine -- in the abdomen near the spine, I found a piece of this explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I inquire whether there's any objection from my learned friend of the tendering into evidence of that photo. The other photo I tend to tender and the doctor's report. I only say it because of the time, it being a couple minutes to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will have an objection, but as to the reasons for our objection I believe it will be more appropriate for me to give you those after the cross-examination. But I am indicating our intention to raise an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, might it just be marked -- might them both be marked for the moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will mark for the moment for identification firstly the report and then the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report will be marked document MFI P70. The photograph document MFI P71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that might be a convenient time, Mr. Re. Doctor, I'm sorry to say that we have come to the end of our day. I appreciate that you have been put to considerable inconvenience, and we regret that. A witness who had previously spent some days here but was not able to conclude her evidence is returning to conclude her evidence at the beginning of our hearing tomorrow. It is not presently clear how long that will take, although it will conclude during tomorrow. It's possible that your evidence could follow and be concluded, but I am not able to assure you of that I'm sorry to say. So it may be that you'll be here until Friday. We will adjourn for the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
